final.title: Design against untested assumptions by narrowing the decision
final.body:
If you want to design against untested assumptions, start by narrowing the decision. For a small business owner, the real question is usually not “can AI do this?” It is: which recurring workflow is frequent enough, measurable enough, and already digital enough to justify a bounded pilot instead of more manual work or another hire.

That is where untested assumptions hide. A demo can look fine and still miss the live questions: who approves what, what data is actually available, and how much handover effort the workflow needs. Human approval still has to stay in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

Bareni’s working rule is simple: work inside the customer’s environment, keep the setup in the customer’s name from the start, and hand over finished code on delivery. That is policy and no-lock-in positioning, not a warranty.

One practical next step is to write down one recurring workflow and note three things: how often it happens, what measurable outcome it should affect, and where the approval point sits. If those are still vague, the assumption is still doing the work for you.

final.title: Design against untested assumptions by narrowing the decision
final.body:
The problem with automation is usually not the tool. It is the hidden assumption behind the workflow.

If you run a small business, the first question is not “Can AI do this?” It is “What exactly is the recurring decision I am trying to change?” That keeps the work bounded. A good candidate is a repetitive task already sitting in digital tools and English-language documents, with a measurable outcome and a clear human owner.

This is where untested assumptions show up. You may assume the data is clean, the approval path is simple, or the handover from manual work to a system will be obvious. In practice, those are separate questions. One demo is not proof that the live workflow will behave the same way.

So the next step is simple: write down one recurring workflow, how often it happens, what “done” means, and where human approval must stay in place. If the decision touches money movement or another high-risk action, the approval stays human.

That narrow view is less exciting than pretending the whole workflow is ready. It is also more useful.
